When you’re showing quotes in a presentation, you’ll often run into issues with leading. In the example below, you’ll notice that the gap between each line is too wide. When you drag the slider, you’ll see how a leading adjustment brings the lines together and makes the quote look cohesive.

If you understand these fundamentals of font choice and typographic spacing, you have enough typography knowledge to build a slide template. All that remains is your slide layouts.

No layout is the best layout

I’ve struggled to adopt slide layouts and failed. In the last decade or so, I’ve found myself rejecting cookie-cutter layouts and starting with a blank slide each time. I follow some slide construction principles, which I’ll show you in a future article, but my template itself is quite simple. When you see my slides, you’ll notice why it’s difficult for me to follow the standard layouts that come with slide templates.

Figure 13: I find it difficult to adapt my design approach to standard slide layouts.

So, I’ve deleted all prescribed layouts that come with our corporate template. My template has three layouts, and I use the blank slide almost all the time. I’ve set up the Thoughtworks corporate palette on my system, so I can choose the colours when I need them for diagrams. I’ve also set up a few font styles based on a serif-and-sans-serif font combination. I use handwritten fonts and monospace fonts on a case-by-case basis, so you won’t see font styles for them. The interaction below will show you different components of my standard presentation theme.

You’ll notice that my template is uncomplicated, and that simplicity lends me a lot of flexibility and power when constructing slides. My slides don’t have page numbers, copyright notices, or even company logos, except on the title slides. Slides are not documents, so slide numbers are irrelevant to my presentations. I don’t want to sue anyone for copying my slides, so I usually leave out the copyright notice. And I want to introduce myself and my employer once at the start and leave it there. From that point on, the logo is an avoidable visual distraction. Taking away these floodmarks (credit: Neal Ford) affords me the luxury of designing an empty slide.

A note about conferences

At conferences, people often photograph your slides. You could add a copyright notice to each slide, but people can remove these floodmarks using phone-based editing apps. I’m not fussed if they reuse the content or design, or if they attribute it to me. So, in the spirit of minimalism, I don’t add a copyright notice. I do announce at the start of the talk that I’ll share a whole bunch of leave-behinds. When I’m taking questions at the end of a talk, I throw up a slide with QR codes (example below), so people who need related resources can access them.

Figure 14: Use QR codes to share resources with your audience.

If you’re concerned about copyright, you can provide a set of watermarked slides through your QR codes. Your slides will be useless without you, but those who want to reference them can have them. The watermarked download will obviate the need for floodmarks on your slides. Win!

A reusable colour palette, a suite of fonts and a blank slide — that’s all you need to address the first decision space in your presentations — that of your template. Once you have that template in place, you can layer components on top of it.

Figure 15: Templates — the first decision space for slide design.

Since we’ve already discussed text and typography in this article, we’ll jump to photographs and illustrations in the next post. I’ll show you how to source images and how to give them a consistent look for your presentation. You’ll also learn how to make text play well with images and how you can avoid some of the most common antipatterns when using images in your slides. See you there.

item.title: Are Harnesses Worth the Cost?
item.description: Naresh Jain compares coding agents building the same API service with and without a behavioral harness. A frontier model, GPT-6 Sol, passed every external evaluation either way. But a cost-optimized model, GPT-6 Luna, succeeded in only 3 of 10 unharnessed runs and all 10 with the harness. While adding the harness increased token usage and runtime for Luna, the harnessed Luna runs achieved the same
item.content:encoded:
I went into this experiment expecting a behavioral harness to help a coding agent meet the requirements more reliably, save tokens and prevent wasted work. Giving an agent clear architectural contracts and deterministic test feedback while it coded seemed like an obvious way to help it get the implementation right on the first pass.

For GPT-6 Sol, the harness used about 10.5 times as many tokens, took nearly 3 times as long, and cost about 7 times more, yet both conditions succeeded in all 10 runs.

The results flatly contradicted that expectation and surprised me. Using Codex with GPT-6 Sol at low reasoning effort, the agent produced an application that passed all 178 automated acceptance tests in each of the 10 runs, both with and without the harness. By this measure, the harness produced no observable improvement in the final applications.

GPT-6 Sol (10-run averages for tokens, time, and cost):

HarnessTokensTimeEstimated costAccepted runsYes11,331,97019 mins 53 secs~$2.67910 of 10No1,076,3716 mins 51 secs~$0.40610 of 10

The harness increased average time and cost without changing the observed acceptance result. In exploratory runs with Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (all at low reasoning effort), each also managed to complete the task unassisted on the first try.

These frontier models handled this task consistently with and without the harness. Could executable feedback help a cost-optimized model achieve similarly consistent outcomes?

Before looking at the results for a cost-optimized model, here is how I set up the experiment:

Experiment setup

Borrowing Birgitta Böckeler’s framing, a behavioral harness combines guides and sensors. Guides anticipate where the agent might go wrong and steer it before it acts, increasing the chance of a correct first attempt. Sensors observe the results after it acts and provide feedback that helps it self-correct.

For each model, I compared agents working with and without the behavioral harness. Both conditions began with the application brief and baseline repository instructions in separate, private workspaces. Harnessed agents also received the API specifications, examples, and tools described in the inner-loop section below.

Figure 1: The two development conditions and their independent evaluation

The experiment separated development from evaluation into two distinct loops. The inner loop provided feedback to harnessed agents while they built. Once an agent finished, the outer loop ran 178 automated acceptance tests against its generated service. Both conditions faced the same evaluation, and the inner harness never had access to the evaluation suite’s answer key. Finally, I collated the accepted outcomes, token use, time, and estimated cost.

In this experiment, I treated an application as acceptable only if it started successfully and passed all 178 external acceptance tests. Reliability meant how consistently a model produced an acceptable application across repeated runs. Token use, elapsed time, and estimated cost were separate measures of run efficiency.

The application brief

Every attempt began with a detailed application brief. I described what the service should do, but left the code-level implementation details to the agent.

The task was to build a backend-for-frontend (BFF) for product discovery. It had to expose a consumer-facing HTTP API, validate incoming requests and downstream responses, and call an Order API. After a successful availability search, it also had to publish only the first returned product to Kafka. Publishing every product would have allowed the agent to pass the data through without implementing the selection behavior.

Figure 2: The application architecture described by the brief

The brief also specified less obvious behavior. A timed-out product creation had to become a deferred request with a 202 response code and a link in the response header that consumers could poll for a response. A transient search failure had to return 429 with a usable recovery interval; unavailable dependencies or failed event publication had to become 503; and successful downstream responses still had to obey requested product filters or otherwise return 502.

Figure 3: A successful availability search and its Kafka publication

In short, the service was more than a set of CRUD endpoints: the agent had to coordinate HTTP semantics, asynchronous events, schema boundaries, and fault-tolerance policies simultaneously.

This was also a favorable starting point for an unaided agent: the brief spelled out the functional requirements, architectural and technology constraints, detailed descriptions of the external interfaces, response shapes, and failure behavior in unusual detail. I do not yet know how the results would change with a less complete brief.

The inner loop: behavioral harness

In this experiment, the guides included OpenAPI and AsyncAPI specifications that expressed the interface agreements in machine-readable form, providing a basis for executable checks. They complemented the brief rather than defining a separate set of requirements. The guides also contained request-response examples for these interfaces. The examples covered downstream timeouts, malformed payloads, filter violations, retry sequences, and Kafka event confirmations. An API-development skill supplied implementation practices and guidance on dependency simulation, behavioral verification, and how to diagnose and respond to failures.

The sensors checked contract conformance, used API tests to verify HTTP response values, and asserted observable side effects, including calls to downstream mocks and Kafka publication. Test results, CTRF reports, and API coverage reports returned those observations to the agent during development.

Birgitta also distinguishes computational controls, executed by deterministic tools, from inferential controls, which rely on model interpretation or judgment. This harness combined both. The behavioral checks produced computational feedback without an LLM judging correctness. Guided by the skill's instructions, the agent still had to interpret those results and decide how to fix failures.

Figure 4: The behavioral harness and its feedback paths

An agent plugin supplied the skill and MCP tools, accompanied by the contracts and examples. The OpenAPI specifications covered the BFF and downstream Order API; the AsyncAPI specification covered Kafka.

Before implementing the service, the agent read the specifications and examples alongside the brief. The skill directed it to map the application’s components and link each required behavior to its downstream interactions and verification checks. Helper scripts scaffolded those documents, a record of verification evidence, and the commands for building, starting, and testing the service; the agent completed the behavior-specific details.

Configuration tools wired the contracts to the application and dependency mocks. Contract-driven dependency mocks made downstream interactions executable, allowing the agent to exercise its implementation against defined downstream responses, failures, and recovery sequences. Other helpers verified timing constraints. Together, these tools provided both implementation guidance and an executable environment in which the agent could check its decisions.

The agent invoked the harness through the project’s test command. That command validated the configuration and examples, ran the required build and unit checks, started the downstream mocks, and launched the application against them. It then ran the checks described above.

Report summaries identified specific contract, response value, and interaction mismatches. The agent used the skill’s instructions to diagnose them, change the implementation or execution setup, and use a helper to rerun the affected scenarios. Once those scenarios passed, the agent ran the complete suite as a final gate. The feedback loop depended on the agent invoking these tools during development; it did not run automatically after every code edit.

Figure 5: The inner-loop test and feedback sequence

Keeping guides and sensors in sync

One of the big challenges of designing this type of behavioral harness is to make sure the guides and sensors don't contradict each other and confuse the agents. I addressed this issue with the following approach:

Before running any tests, an “examples validate” command checked that the example payloads complied with the respective API specifications. Tests then used those specifications and examples to check the implementation, keeping the sensors aligned with their source guides.

The source of those checks mattered. If an agent interprets requirements to write both the implementation and its tests, the same misreading or omission can appear in both. Allowing it to change the expected results when tests fail can also obscure a defect. Here, the contracts and examples represent agreed human expectations in executable form. Contract checks were generated deterministically from supplied specifications, while supplied examples with behavioral fixtures defined value and side-effect assertions. The agent was instructed to preserve those inputs and the skill’s verification helpers, investigate failures, and correct the implementation or execution setup rather than weaken the expectations.

This gave verification expectations a source independent of the implementing agent’s interpretation. Used as a deterministic computational control, they make correctness checkable without relying on the agent's own claims or an LLM's judgment, freeing humans to focus review on what the contracts don't cover.

The same sensors therefore serve two distinct purposes depending on when they run:

  • During development: Sensor results feed back to the agent as executable attention, steering construction and helping it recover from lapses.
  • At completion: Sensor results become the basis for accepting the work: an independent check of the agent's interpretation against human expectations, which matters for every model.

The skill also required reviewable evidence of dependency interactions and the final verification result, so completion was supported by recorded observations rather than the agent’s claim alone.

In this experiment, I implemented the behavioral harness using Specmatic, though equivalent contract-testing and service virtualization tools could provide the same capabilities.

The outer loop: evaluation harness

To keep the comparison fair, each attempt ran inside an isolated Docker container with its own workspace and a fresh, attempt-specific Codex home. Apart from shared authentication and language dependency caches, each agent began without sessions, memories, plugins, skills, or other state from an earlier run.

The two conditions differed in what agents could use during development; within each comparison, completed applications faced the same external evaluation.

After development stopped, the outer-loop evaluation harness tested each application against the same corpus of 178 combined functional checks, including invalid inputs, downstream failures, recovery sequences, and the messages produced by successful requests. These checks exercised the behavior specified in the application brief, including the client-facing API, downstream interactions, and Kafka publication. The evaluation harness controlled its own downstream fixtures and message capture rather than relying on the application's development tests.

Testing a cost-optimized model

OpenAI positions GPT-6 Sol as a flagship model for complex professional work, while GPT-6 Luna is optimized for cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads and roughly corresponds to the nano tier in earlier GPT-5 families.

With the methodology in place, the core question is whether a model with a smaller capability profile would behave differently.

I ran the exact same experiment on GPT-6 Luna at low reasoning effort. Without a harness, it succeeded in 3 of 10 runs. With the harness, it succeeded in all 10.

GPT-6 Luna (10-run averages for tokens, time, and cost):

HarnessTokensTimeEstimated costAccepted runsYes22,933,64835 mins~$0.27310 of 10No5,860,73615 mins 56 secs~$0.0863 of 10

In this sample, the harness did not unlock a capability Luna lacked; it turned a 3-in-10 baseline into 10-for-10 reliability.

Providing that feedback added an average of 17,072,912 tokens, 19 minutes 4 seconds of autonomous runtime, and about $0.187 of estimated API-equivalent cost per attempt. The harnessed attempt used roughly 3.9 times as many tokens overall as an unharnessed Luna attempt. But look at the comparative economics: even with the harness overhead, a harnessed Luna attempt cost about 33% less than an unharnessed Sol attempt ($0.273 vs $0.406), and both conditions achieved the same 10-for-10 acceptance rate in this sample.

What went better than expected

Looking past the headline pass rates into the codebase, several implementations stood out:

  • GPT-6 Sol solved the brief unaided in one shot.

    A single /goal prompt was enough. All 10 unharnessed GPT-6 Sol applications passed every functional check on the first pass without human debugging or corrective follow-ups.

  • GPT-6 Luna came remarkably close on its own.

    Unharnessed GPT-6 Luna runs passed 94.8% of the functional checks. It was stumbling over subtle edge cases rather than missing the task entirely.

  • Asynchronous 202 workflows held together end-to-end.

    Returning a 202 Accepted status code is straightforward. What surprised me was seeing the agent wire up the monitor endpoint, track pending requests, retry downstream creation with the original idempotency key, and surface the final payload at the polling URL.

  • Kafka publication stayed tied to the search transaction.

    Rather than firing off a message asynchronously and returning an immediate 200, accepted applications waited for Kafka acknowledgement before responding, and correctly translated publication failures or timeouts into 503 Service Unavailable.

  • Boundary validation was consistently defensive.

    Both models validated incoming payloads against schemas and validated downstream response structures and business constraints before using the data, rather than blindly trusting downstream services.

Where unharnessed runs slipped up

The failed unharnessed Java applications did not contain invalid syntax or fundamentally misunderstand the brief. Each still passed at least 144 of the 178 combined functional checks. Their failures clustered around the deferred creation workflow and a smaller set of protocol details:

The observed gaps appeared at protocol boundaries, resiliency paths, and integration seams, where a convincing implementation could still fail as a system.

  • Deferred creation broke at the timeout boundary.

    When a downstream product creation exceeded the configured timeout, the BFF was supposed to return 202 Accepted with a monitor link, retry in the background, and eventually expose the downstream 201 response. Instead, 4 unharnessed applications returned 503, 2 returned 400, and 1 returned 429. An application already counted above also created monitors in some scenarios, but its retries never reached the terminal 201 response. Several implementations recognized timeouts by matching a narrow exception type or cause-chain shape. The artifacts establish the incorrect responses, but often do not record the actual client exception, so that mechanism is a likely explanation rather than a proven common cause.

  • Missing monitor links caused secondary failures.

    In 7 runs, the incorrect response to the timed-out creation also meant that no monitor URL was returned. A later evaluator check then failed while trying to use that missing URL. I treat those errors as consequences of the broken 202 flow, not as separate application defects.

  • Kafka delivery succeeded while contract conformance failed.

    In 3 runs, every expected message reached Kafka, but the evaluator still rejected the publication. Two applications used Spring's JSON serializer and added an unexpected __TypeId__ header. Another emitted “categories”: null, even though the optional field had to contain an array when present. The integration worked mechanically while still violating the wire contract.

  • Error responses missed exact HTTP contracts.

    Other observed misses were narrower. Although 415 Unsupported Media Type is a conventional response for an unsupported media type, the application brief explicitly required 400 for invalid requests of this kind, so the evaluator counted 415 as a contract violation. In other cases, invalid requests reached a generic 500 handler, and a missing monitor returned the wrong representation. These were small differences in code, but enough to make the application unacceptable under the external evaluation.

  • Configuration names diverged at an integration seam.

    Ordinary product creation returned 503 instead of 201. The generated client read ORDER_API_API_KEY, while the recorded launch supplied ORDER_API_KEY. That mismatch is a plausible explanation for the downstream failures. In harnessed runs, contract-driven dependency mocks and configuration checks enabled validations of these environment variables before deployment.

The harness as executable attention

A behavioral harness turns written requirements into environmental feedback, bringing dropped details back into focus when a sensor goes red.

I find myself thinking about this dynamic in terms of executable attention.

The behaviors behind these failures were specified in the supplied requirements. The application brief clearly specified the deferred creation workflow, Kafka message contract, and exact error responses. A requirement can be explicit in the brief and still lose influence during implementation. I think of this as an attention lapse: the resulting code omits or incompletely implements a requirement the agent was given.

Juggling library choices, boilerplate setup, dependency injection, and asynchronous wiring across a growing context may contribute to such lapses, although this experiment did not establish the cause. Executable attention makes those gaps observable, giving the agent another opportunity to act on the requirement.

  • A timed-out creation isn't deferred until the response includes a monitor link and polling eventually reaches the downstream result.
  • A Kafka publication isn't valid merely because a message arrived; its payload and headers must both conform to the wire contract.
  • An optional field cannot be serialized as null when the contract permits only an array or omission.
  • An error response isn't correct unless its status, content type, and body all match the client-facing contract.

GPT-6 Sol preserved these details from the written brief in all observed runs. GPT-6 Luna also implemented much of the behavior correctly without the harness, but its accepted outcomes varied. The misses in Luna are consistent with requirements losing influence during implementation. My interpretation is that the harness served as an external memory and attention aid, pulling dropped requirements back into focus whenever a sensor went red.

The economics of consistent outcomes

Putting both model samples side by side makes the cost of that feedback visible. These are API-equivalent estimates based on recorded token use and model prices, not actual billed costs.

Figure 6: Average estimated cost and time across both models

Within the GPT-6 runs, harnessed Luna averaged about $0.273 per attempt, compared with $0.406 for unharnessed Sol; both had 10 accepted applications in 10 attempts. The harnessed Luna attempt therefore cost about 33% less on average in this sample.

All 10 harnessed GPT-6 Luna applications passed the external evaluation and achieved a 100% success rate. This small sample cannot tell us the long-run failure rate or the total cost of achieving an acceptable application.

These figures measure only autonomous generation cost and machine time. They exclude the upfront effort of authoring, reviewing, and maintaining the contracts, examples, assertions, and harness. They also leave out the effort of finding, diagnosing, and repairing an unacceptable result. Reusing interface contracts and checks across implementations could spread the setup cost over time, but I did not measure that reuse or the resulting total cost.

Sol’s 10-for-10 result still depended on independent evaluation. That suggests another comparison: make the sensors available to the agent only at a final verification gate, rather than throughout development. A final-gate workflow would provide an independent acceptance check while minimizing overhead when the first implementation passes. Failures, however, could still require diagnosis and repair cycles. I did not measure that workflow’s cost.

The boundaries of this experiment

This experiment covered 10 paired runs per model on 1 greenfield Java service, with both models at low reasoning effort. That sample describes the observed outcomes; it cannot establish long-run reliability.

A more demanding architecture or a trickier resiliency scenario might expose gaps in Sol that require a harness. Conversely, a simpler task might run reliably on Luna without this behavioral harness.

The brief specified functional behavior, architecture, technology, and interfaces in unusual detail. I have not tested whether the pattern holds when modifying legacy code, using other languages or reasoning settings, or working from vague or incomplete requirements. A less complete brief could affect both the unaided implementation and the quality of the contracts and examples supplied to the harness. I would be cautious about extrapolating these exact figures to different briefs, architectures, codebases, or team workflows.

Because the harness added guides and sensors together, this experiment also cannot isolate their individual contributions.

What this means in practice

I would treat these results as a starting point for choosing a model and feedback cadence for a particular task. What changes with model capability is when and how often the sensors run, not whether an independent check is needed.

Model capability changes when and how often sensors run, not whether an independent verification gate is needed.

  • For cost-optimized models: When a cost-optimized model produces inconsistent results, run a behavioral harness throughout development. It serves as executable attention, catching drift as it happens and turning inconsistent attempts into dependable delivery.
  • For frontier models: Retain an independent acceptance check even when a model passes consistently on the first attempt. Instead of running continuous checks during development, run the automated tests once as a deterministic final verification gate before acceptance, providing an independent check with minimal overhead.
  • Invest in clear specifications and examples: The checks can enforce only the expectations humans encode. Review and maintain those expectations alongside the implementation, and use human review to address gaps in coverage.

Conclusion

My original assumption was too blunt. A behavioral harness is not an automatic win for every model on every task. For Sol, running the harness throughout development added overhead without a detected acceptance benefit; for Luna, harnessed attempts were accepted more consistently and cost less on average than unharnessed Sol attempts in this sample.

That leaves me with a revised, conditional hypothesis:

What changes with model capability is not whether independent sensors are needed, but when they run. For models whose unaided attempts produce inconsistent outcomes, running sensors continuously during development provides executable attention that broadens the set of models a team can use successfully. For frontier models capable of solving the brief in one pass, running those same sensors once as an independent final acceptance gate provides the verification every system requires without the development overhead.

In practice, engineering teams rarely pick a model on raw benchmark intelligence alone. Unit economics, latency budgets, data privacy, and the ability to run on premises often dominate the decision. If a behavioral harness can take a cheaper, lighter model that already fits those operational constraints and make it reliably deliver the goods, that is a compelling option.

I have tested this so far on a single greenfield service with an unusually detailed brief. The next step is to test a “final gate only” condition for frontier models to measure its overhead and how often the gate catches discrepancies. Beyond that, I plan to vary the quality of the brief and the consequences of a missed requirement, then test how well this hypothesis holds up when modifying an existing codebase, switching programming languages, or running open-weights models locally.

item.title: The Craft of Practitioner Voice
item.description: A couple of months ago Jim Highsmith explained how practitioners writing for each other forms a distinct style of writing. He now adds a section to the article with more detail on the craft of how we write in this style. How the writer shows up in the prose, its four principles, the role of story, how to sensibly use AI, three levels of editing, and clarity of the audience.
item.content:encoded:
The Craft of Practitioner Voice

Practitioner Voice is not a tone. It is a discipline: start with the claim, stay visible, ground authority in consequence, compress without losing meaning, and leave real tension live. The goal is not to sound more personal. The goal is to make earned judgment useful to readers who have lived the problem.

The category existed before it had a name. Practitioners have been writing this way for years, on Substack, on martinfowler.com, in Cutter journals, in the margins of conference papers, and finding their way to it by instinct or luck. A good editor. An encouraging colleague. Someone who said: let your voice out. Without the category there were no guidelines. Without guidelines practitioners defaulted to the two models they knew: academic scaffolding or thought leadership polish. This piece is the beginning of guidelines that should have existed.

How to use AI without losing your voice

A year ago, I started thinking of it as alternative intelligence rather than artificial intelligence. Intelligence without consciousness: a different kind of mind, not a lesser one. That reframe matters for how you work with it.

How writers use AI, and what they owe their readers about it, is still unsettled. Two practitioners I respect have landed in opposite places.

Mik Kersten writes: “I decided to write every word in this book and did not use AI for any of the ideating, outlining, or writing. The writing process helped me slow down and contemplate, and I hope the process of reading this book will do the same for you.” The writing process itself is the point. AI would have short-circuited it. Mik’s approach would please William Zinsser, who wrote: “Writing is a form of thinking, whatever the subject.” AI makes it possible to produce without learning. That’s the trap.

Jurgen Appelo takes the opposite position. He wrote with a team of one human and multiple AI agents: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others. Some sections originated with him; others started with the agents and he refined them. His argument: creativity has always been collaborative. AI is the latest in a long lineage of tools that amplify human capacity. What matters is the experience the reader gets, not who or what generated each sentence.

Both positions are principled. I landed somewhere else.

Parkinson’s changed my cognitive processing. Not all at once. A word that used to surface instantly now takes a beat longer. A thread of argument that once held itself in working memory needs an external anchor. Sixty years of consequence-bearing experience didn’t disappear. The pattern recognition I built across careers in software development, management consulting, and organizational leadership stayed. What changed was the biological system I’d always run it through.

Parkinson’s is my version of a universal condition. Every practitioner has something: attention that fragments under pressure, memory that loses threads, processing that slows with fatigue, language that doesn’t always surface on demand. The biological system we run our judgment through is never perfect. AI, designed well, augments what each of us needs. The discipline is the same regardless of what you’re augmenting: keep the judgment constitutive, or the writing stops being yours.

I started working with AI the way most people do: as a tool. Draft this. Summarize that. Speed up what I was already doing. That lasted six months. Then something shifted. I was in the middle of a complex argument, the kind that used to hold itself together through a long writing session, and I noticed the AI wasn’t helping me execute the thinking. I was thinking through it. My judgment, my pattern authority, my accumulated perspective finding its way forward through an architecture that could hold what my working memory no longer reliably sustained. The argument didn’t happen inside me and get recorded. It happened across both minds.

That was the moment the tool became something else.

Andy Clark and David Chalmers called this the extended mind, proposed as philosophy in 1998, arrived at out of necessity in my case in 2024. They offered a thought experiment. Otto has Alzheimer’s and uses a notebook the way others use biological memory. The conventional view says the notebook is a tool. Clark and Chalmers argue it is part of Otto’s cognitive system, coupled in a direct, here-and-now causal loop. Thinking happens across both. Otto directs his notebook. The notebook does not direct Otto. That asymmetry is everything.

The coupling can build the practitioner or quietly replace them. I developed a test and kept returning to it: is this judgment I earned, or fluency I accepted? It doesn’t catch everything. It catches enough.

That distinction shapes every interaction with AI. Treat AI output as first material, not final material. Use it for structure, contrast, and clarity testing. Use it to find the gaps in your own argument. Do not let it finalize voice. A practitioner who defers judgment to AI one interaction at a time loses the capacity to exercise it independently. The skill erodes quietly, below the threshold of awareness, until the moment it’s needed most.

Augmentation builds the practitioners. Automation replaces them.

What the writer brings

In the first part of this essay, I established where pattern authority comes from. The craft question is how it shows up in the prose.

Practitioner authority rests on consequence-bearing experience, not credential. Academic authority comes from method and institutional affiliation. Thought leadership authority comes from platform size and reputation management. Practitioner authority comes from having been responsible for an outcome, not studying it, not advising on it from a safe distance, but owning what happened next. That weight shows in every sentence or it doesn’t show at all. You can’t install it and you can’t fake it.

This holds whether you write about surgery, software, organizational change, or bridge design. The field is incidental. The relationship to consequence is not.

For consultants the authority takes a different form. Few of us carry direct accountability for outcomes. But years of proximity to consequence, watching patterns across organizations, being trusted with decisions you don’t formally own, learning whose experience to trust and why, builds something real. You know what good judgment looks like under pressure because you’ve watched it fail and succeed across dozens of organizations. That’s not the same as owning the outcome. It’s not nothing either. Earned differently. Still earned.

That different foundation creates a different contract with the reader. Academic-essayistic writing builds the scaffolding first: define, contextualize, qualify, then deploy. Practitioner Voice drops a term into a lived context and trusts the reader to close the gap from their own experience. The scaffolding isn’t missing. The reader is the scaffolding.

Show the scar. The practitioner who has only succeeded has limited range. The one who has failed, learned, and kept going has the full picture. Academic writing contains failure in a limitations section, safely quarantined from the argument. Thought leadership avoids failure entirely; it undermines the brand. Practitioner Voice uses failure as a source of credibility. The scar is the credential. Ground your authority in consequence, not in the degrees on the wall.

Staying visible is harder than it sounds. The framework, the data, the existing literature — these earn their place when they serve your judgment. They become camouflage when they replace it. Your judgment is the point. Stay in the frame.

How the form works

One practical technique before you start: write the back cover first. For a book, this forces three questions before a single chapter exists: who is this for, what will they get from it, and why does it matter now. For an article, write the LinkedIn lede first. Same discipline, different form. If you can’t state the claim in three sentences for a practitioner audience, the piece isn’t ready to draft.

Four principles define how Practitioner Voice works on the page:

Start with the claim. Academic writing earns the conclusion through evidence, argument, and qualification. Practitioner Voice opens with the conclusion and “lets the rest of the piece be explanation, not proof. If the reader has lived the pattern they’ll recognize the claim immediately. If they haven’t, no amount of scaffolding will convince them. Trust the reader to close the gap.

Compression as respect. Write as if the reader already knows more than they can easily articulate. Fewer definitions. Shorter transitions. Declarative statements over explanatory ones. Space between ideas. If something feels obvious to an experienced practitioner, don’t apologize for that; let recognition do the work. Completeness is optional. Resonance is not.

Inspiration and information, blended. Practitioners often write as if these are separate: lead with a story, then deliver the lesson; open with a hook, then provide the data. Practitioner Voice doesn’t separate them. The information arrives inside the inspiration. The insight carries the evidence with it. When it works, the reader doesn’t experience a gear shift from engaging to informative. The piece stays in one register throughout because the judgment and the data are inseparable. If you find yourself writing a section that is purely inspirational or purely informational, that’s the signal. Blend it back.

Consider the tension between Mik Kersten and Jurgen Appelo earlier in this piece. One wrote every word himself; the other co-wrote with a team of AI agents. Both positions are principled. Both carry risk. Naming that tension without collapsing it gives the reader something more useful than either answer alone.

Leaving tension live is harder than it sounds. Name it. Illuminate it. Step back. Do not resolve it for the reader; resolving it would be lying. The tension is real and the reader must navigate it themselves. This is the closing constraint that separates Practitioner Voice from every other professional writing form. Academic writing resolves tension in the conclusion. Thought leadership resolves it in the three takeaways. Practitioner Voice leaves it live because that’s where the judgment lives.

Story: the mechanism that makes ideas move

Facts inform. Arguments persuade. Stories move people to act.

Chip and Dan Heath put it plainly: “A credible idea makes people believe. An emotional idea makes people care. The right story makes people act.” That hierarchy matters for practitioners who write. Most professional writing stops at credible. Practitioner Voice reaches for all three.

Consider the Agile Manifesto, one of the stickiest ideas in software history. The value, “working software over comprehensive documentation”, has been cited, debated, and misapplied for more than twenty years. What made it stick? It was simple without being simplistic, a complex idea in direct language that guides action without prescribing it. It was unexpected; until then, methodologies emphasized architecture and design, and code just followed blueprints. It was concrete; anyone in the software business immediately knows what working software means. It carried credibility from recognized practitioners. It carried emotion for developers exhausted by failing traditional methods.

And it had a story. The Snowbird ski resort. Seventeen people in a room. A manifesto written in two days. That origin narrative has been retold thousands of times. The story of how the idea was born is often stickier than the idea itself.

Practitioners underestimate the power of story. We get tangled in technology and methodology, facts and figures, analysis and concepts. Good ideas get neglected because we fail to engage people emotionally as well as intellectually. A story doesn’t decorate an argument. It is the argument’s delivery mechanism, the thing that makes the reader feel tension before they understand it.

Practitioner Voice is built for this. The scar is a story. The moment of recognition is a story. The project that failed, the client who pushed back, the decision that turned out wrong; these are not digressions from the argument. They are the argument, carried in narrative form. Show the scar is a storytelling instruction as much as a credibility instruction.

Stories don’t have to come from the conference room. A mountaineering moment, a physical consequence, a landscape that forced a decision; these carry the same authority as a project war story, sometimes more. The terrain metaphor earns its place in Practitioner Voice because it connects abstract judgment to embodied experience. Readers who have never managed a software project have still stood at the edge of something uncertain and had to decide.

Craft the story before you craft the argument. Know what happened, who was there, what the stakes were, and what changed. Then build the argument around it. The story is not the illustration. It is the foundation.

Structure: braided narrative

Most professional writing defaults to one of two structures: chronological or logical. Chronological moves through time. Logical moves through argument, problem to solution, claim to evidence. Both are serviceable. Neither is the only option.

The braided narrative weaves multiple threads simultaneously, each developing independently while reinforcing the others. A reader follows several strands at once, and the meaning emerges from their intersection rather than from a single linear argument. The structure is common in literary nonfiction and almost unknown in technical and management writing, which is exactly why it’s worth naming here. It is more difficult to execute than either chronological or logical structure. When it works, it is more rewarding than either.

My Wild West to Agile uses five braids across four eras of software development:

  • The evolution of methods and methodologies
  • Personal experiences and growth across six decades
  • The pioneers who drove each era forward
  • The explosion of technology innovation
  • The progressive management trends that shaped the field

No single braid carries the book. The argument lives in how they weave together.

John Willis’s Rebels of Reason combines braided narrative with chronology: a spine running from Aristotle to ChatGPT with multiple threads running through it, philosophical, technical, and biographical. The chronology orients the reader. The braids create the texture and the surprise.

The braided narrative suits Practitioner Voice because it keeps tension live across multiple dimensions simultaneously. No single thread resolves while the others are still running. The reader holds several things at once, which is closer to how experienced practitioners think than any single-thread argument allows.

When to consider braids: when your subject has more than one dimension that can’t be subordinated to a single argument without losing something essential. When you find yourself writing parallel tracks and forcing them into sequence, that’s the signal. The braids want to run together.

Three levels of editing

The most common editing mistake is fixing the spelling before the argument is worth saving. I once coached a colleague on his first book. He would write a paragraph, then polish it to death before moving to the next. The momentum never built. I kept pushing him to write more and write faster, get the argument down before refining the sentences. It wasn’t his natural style. He resisted, then adapted. The book got finished and published. The polish habit didn’t kill the book. It nearly did.

Mixing levels too early distracts from the work that matters most at each stage. Three levels of editing serve different purposes and need to happen in sequence.

Developmental editing (challenges thinking). It looks at the piece as a whole: purpose, argument, structure, audience, flow, missing ideas, weak logic, and unnecessary material. The goal is to strengthen thinking and architecture before polishing the prose. Claims that may eventually need support should be flagged, but citation mechanics and reference formatting should not derail development before the argument has settled. Key question: does this work as a piece of writing?

Line Editing (improves the writing). It works at paragraph and sentence level to improve clarity, flow, emphasis, voice, rhythm, transitions, word choice, and concision without changing the core argument. Each paragraph should carry a clear idea, develop it coherently, and connect naturally to what comes before and after. Key question: does each paragraph carry one clear idea, and does the language say what I mean in the way I want to say it?

Proofreading (cleans up the writing). It catches grammar, spelling, punctuation, typos, formatting inconsistencies, and other mechanical errors. This is also the right stage for a final check of citations, references, links, and source formatting. Key question: is this clean, correct, and ready to publish?

One rule on citations: identify gaps early, fix mechanics late. The point is not to ignore evidence. It is to keep the reference apparatus from becoming the tail that wags the article. First make sure the argument deserves to survive. Then make the citations impeccable. Citation placement breaks the train of thought at the moment it matters most. Name the source naturally in prose when it’s relevant, put the full reference at the end, and trust the reader to follow up if they want to.

Citations also exist out of respect for other writers. Years ago I was reading an article online. The further I read, the more familiar it felt. I pulled out my Agile Software Development Ecosystems book and found the entire article copied word for word from one of my chapters. No reference. No attribution. That was more than a citation failure. That was plagiarism. Citations exist because ideas belong to people. Put them at the end so they don’t interrupt the reading. But put them in.

Word choice and context calibration

Simple words are not weak words. They are precise words that don’t require the reader to translate. Every technical term should earn its place by doing something a plain word cannot. When a simpler word exists, use it. When the technical term is the right tool, use that. The test is precision, not prestige.

Before you calibrate the vocabulary, identify the reader. Your target audience is narrower than you think. The more precisely you can picture the person reading this, the easier every word choice becomes.

Context calibration is the deeper skill, and it applies to every vocabulary choice a practitioner makes. A cardiologist telling a colleague that a patient presented with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis uses precise shorthand among people trained to receive it. She tells the family the lungs are scarring and breathing will keep getting harder. Same condition, same doctor, same precision, different context. The clinical vocabulary doesn’t disappear. It stays where it belongs. Before reaching for any term, technical or otherwise, the practitioner asks: does this reader share the context that makes this word useful? If yes, use it. If not, translate.

The same discipline applies to consultant vocabulary. “Organizational agility” in a room full of practitioners who live inside that definition is efficient shorthand; everyone knows you mean how fast we can change direction without breaking and saying it the long way wastes their time. The same term dropped into an executive briefing without translation becomes camouflage; it signals tribal membership instead of transferring meaning. The first time you use a term with a mixed audience, define it once in plain language, briefly, then move. After that the shorthand is earned. Context calibration isn’t a prohibition on professional vocabulary. It’s the judgment call that determines when vocabulary serves the reader and when it serves only the writer.

Here is what that looks like in practice. A recent draft contained this sentence: “The contracting model prices the surface and is silent on the substrate, not because the substrate doesn’t matter, but because it was never in the model. It is the same blind spot as your dashboard, in peer-reviewed form.” Correct, precise, and written for an audience that will stop and work through the sentence.

Rewritten for a practitioner: “The contracting model measures what it can see and misses what it can’t. Same blind spot as your dashboard. Just peer-reviewed.” Same idea. One beat of support. Reader closes the gap. That is the difference, and it is not a cosmetic one.

At the sentence level:

  • Use active verbs. Reduce “is” and “was”; build sentences around what things do, not what they are.
  • Minimize gerunds ending in -ing where a direct verb works better.
  • Use “that” sparingly.
  • Plan sentence lengths deliberately; short sentences accelerate, long ones slow the reader down.
  • A period is a stop sign. A colon announces something ahead. A dash is a tree branch in the road. Use each one knowing what it does to the reader’s pace.

Who you write for

Knowing who you write for changes every sentence. Academics write for peer reviewers. Thought leadership writes for eyeballs. Practitioner Voice writes for people who have lived the pattern and will recognize it when someone states it plainly. You are not writing for everyone. You are writing for the reader who has lived this pattern or will. Close enough to recognize it when they do. Far enough out that your experience arrives before theirs does.

Practitioner Voice is comfortable with limited context. This worked here, under these conditions; judge for yourself whether it fits your situation. That’s a different contract with the reader than academic or thought leadership writing offers. Both push toward universal claims: academic writing for impact factor, thought leadership for audience size. Practitioner Voice trusts specificity. A piece that says “here’s what I saw and what I concluded, in this context,” is more honest and often more useful than one dressed up as universal truth.

A piece is as long as the tension requires and no longer. Short is not a virtue; unnecessary length is a failure.

Most pieces earn a carry phrase: a closing line that sticks. Not a summary. A reorientation. The reader finishes thinking: yes, that’s the tension I’ve been living with. Not every structure calls for it. The inverted pyramid lets the reader exit once they have what they need. But when the form allows it, know what line you’re building toward before you write the opening.

The category now has a name. The Practitioner Voice now has craft guidelines. What it still needs is practitioners willing to write this way, to stay in the frame, show the scar, and trust the reader to close the gap.

That part can’t be outlined.

Reactions, pushbacks, and examples from your own practice are welcome. The conversation is on LinkedIn.

item.title: Principles for effective slides
item.description: Not every presentation needs slides, but when they earn their place, they work as a visual channel that complements the speaker rather than replacing them. Sumeet Gayathri Moghe sets out the principles that follow from that idea — control over the rate of knowledge exposition, tight coupling between slides and speaker, minimalism by default, visuals that say more than words can, and never sending
item.content:encoded:
By now, we’ve established the need for a strong narrative before you build slides. Not every presentation needs slides. Once you’ve built your narrative, you may decide that a speech is good enough. In fact, a few months back, I did just that. I was a leader-in-residence at our graduate program, Thoughtworks University. The trainers expected me to deliver a keynote, and I decided against slides. I called the talk “1% better — three things I wish I'd known as a grad.” 15 minutes, no visuals, just talk. And that was fine! The world didn’t end because a corporate talk didn’t have slides.

You may work at a corporation where no conversation can begin without a slide deck on the screen. I’ve found this reliance on slides unproductive, especially when the cognitive load of frameworks sabotages the high-bandwidth collaboration possible when smart people find themselves in a synchronous space.

All this said, I’m also an unabashed advocate for effective slides. Many presenters underestimate their content, thinking their topic is dull and that nothing will make it interesting. That may be true for a minority of topics. In which case, why are you even presenting? In most cases, you believe that your topic is interesting enough that you want to change something for your audience. You may want to sell a product, advocate for a new way of working, teach them something new, or motivate and inspire them. This is where your narrative can benefit from impactful visuals.

While design and decoration aren’t the same thing, you also want your visuals to look good.

Attractive things make people feel good, which in turn makes them think more creatively…positive emotions are critical to learning, curiosity, and creative thought.

-- Don Norman

With that context behind us, let’s unpack when slides are most useful for presentations and the fundamental principles for building them.

Use slides as a complementary visual channel

If you examine the light table (a.k.a. slide sorter) view of my slide decks, they won’t make sense to you. Without my narrative, they’re useless. And yet, the slides employ the same components that an infodeck might.

  • Colours, typography, and slide layouts that determine the overall template;
  • and multiple components that include but aren’t limited to:
    • text;
    • images and illustrations;
    • diagrams;
    • charts;
    • and videos.

Figure 1: Slides from a past talk.

The most important distinction between a presentation and an infodeck is what Neal Ford calls “control over the rate of knowledge exposition.” Unlike static infodecks, the builds (animations) and transitions in your presentation slides allow you to control that rate of knowledge exposition. You get to manage your audience’s cognitive load.

Slides also provide what Martin Fowler calls a “complementary visual channel” for your presentation. As a speaker, you’re conveying a message to your audience. The most important part of that message comes from your voice, expertise and stage presence. The slides shouldn’t make you redundant. Instead, they should enrich the message you’re already sharing using the audio channel.

Figure 2: You provide the words. The slides provide the visuals and some reinforcing words.

The idea of a complementary visual channel becomes even more important when you reflect on how we learn. In their 2016 book, E-Learning and the Science of Instruction, Clark and Mayer establish the “multimedia principle”; i.e. people learn better from words and graphics than from words alone. We encode words and visuals in different parts of our brains. When you provide the words and your slides provide the visuals, your audience benefits from dual coding. Your message becomes more memorable than if you provided words alone, or worse, words similar to those on your slide.

Slides aren’t the only visual channel possible. Tools like Prezi, Mural and Miro let you create a giant canvas for your talk, and you can pan and zoom into specific parts of it to support your presentation. However, since slideware is more ubiquitous in corporations, we’ll focus on the 16x9 slide format for the rest of our discussion.

Couple slides tightly with the speaker

When we think of slides as the visual channel for our presentations, another principle becomes apparent — your visuals must tightly couple with what you’ll say, without repeating what you’ll say. After all, you’ll present to a literate audience, and they can read faster than you read aloud.

Take a look at the slide below. It’s an example of the standard-issue slides you’ll see in a corporate infodeck. As a standalone reading artefact, it’s passable. As a presentation slide, it’s a disaster. By the time you start with the first point, your audience will have already speed-read the entire page. Martin Fowler calls this phenomenon “stealing the narrative,” because slides like these make you lose control of your story.

Figure 3: Audiences can read such slides faster than you.

The above slide is an example of why you can’t present an infodeck, no matter how elegant the design. Don’t beat yourself up when your eyes glaze over at the sight of such slides. The above example also raises the question of why you’re there in the first place.

If the slides can stand by themselves, why are you up there in front of them? Just hand out the slides and sit down!

-- David S. Rose, venture capitalist

What’s the alternative, then? If I were presenting the content on the slide above, I’d break up the visuals to match my narrative. The single slide above would split into the 31 visuals below, driven by slide transitions and animations. The words on screen will appear as a summary of what I say, either in sync with my speech or right after I’ve made my point.

Now, if you were the narrator, you might choose a different split. Therein lies the disadvantage of well-designed slides that serve as a complementary visual channel. It’s difficult to share your slides with someone so they can present your topic. Effective slides often reinforce a speaker’s storytelling style, pace, and anecdotes. They’re fine-tuned to the speaker’s idiosyncrasies. While you can use another speaker’s slides, you’ll have to tune them to your delivery approach.

Practise minimalism by default

When you design slides that are in sync with your speech, you can’t design heavy, wordy slides. A single slide can have many elements, but you must control the rate at which you reveal those elements, so you don’t let your audience race ahead of you. So, I suggest being minimalist by default when constructing your slides. Take Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's quote to heart.

Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.

-- Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

When designing slides for your presentation, think in snapshots and be ruthless about how little each snapshot reveals and how much it adds to a previous snapshot. Invariably, you’ll end up with a deck with many slides, and as I’ve said earlier in the series, the number of slides doesn’t matter.

The example below will help make my point. These are slides I presented to a C-suite audience to explain developer relations. It took me two minutes to get through 14 snapshots, all related to the same base diagram. When you thumb through the slides, you’ll see that I reveal each part of the framework in a new snapshot. I then overlay the diagram with an example of that aspect of developer relations, then move back to the main diagram and reveal the next aspect.

Designing the slides this way enabled me to manage my audience’s cognitive load and the rate at which I presented information.

To practice minimalism, think of slides as billboards. In her book, slide:ology, Nancy Duarte says that slides are “glance media” and share much in common with billboards. You want each visual or snapshot to be easy to grok in a few seconds. If a billboard takes too long to understand, it could cause an accident on the street. If a slide takes too long to process, well, you might have a cognitive accident to deal with.

Figure 4: Slides have a lot in common with billboards.

Treat slides as integrated visuals

If your audience is thinking about your slides, they’re not paying attention to your message. This is why I never let anyone else control my slides. “Next slide, please” is the easiest way to distract your audience from the message and have them think about your slides.

The most effective slides often don’t feel like a collection of components. They feel like integrated visuals that, along with the speaker, create a cinematic presentation experience. The audience doesn’t sense how one slide transitions to another or how you’re using layers and builds in your visuals, and they shouldn’t have to. Here’s a three-minute video presentation that may help make my point.

The above presentation is simple. It uses only a few icons, text and images. But it’s difficult to say where one slide begins and another ends. And that’s by design. The more continuity we create across our slides, the less salient the number of slides and their construction. The less salient these inner workings are, the more salient our narrative can be.

Use the visual channel to say a thousand words

A year or so back, I delivered a short talk about AI and a “perpetual beta” mindset. I won’t get into the details of the talk, but I’ll walk you through the slides below. In my presentation, I explained how AI models on cameras use a split-second heuristic to autofocus on a subject's eyes — human or animal. I then cycled through many subjects the camera eye-detects with ease and said, “What happens when an animal has eyes all over their body?” On cue, a leopard’s photo appeared on screen. The audience could see why the camera fails to autofocus. That punchline, combined with the blurry photo of a leopard, got me a good laugh from the audience and helped me make the point that even mature AI is fallible.

When you deliver a presentation, you often assume the role of an educator. Visuals can help you add a layer of entertainment to your education. Notice how little text I use in the above example. I let the photographs do most of the talking. At the end of the segment, one of the photos also adds comic relief. 13 slides, a minute of talking, and 13 photos that say more than I ever could without the slides.

This isn’t to say that text is unnecessary. Text can reinforce or summarise what you say and help you label parts of the visual. Saying a picture speaks a thousand words doesn’t mean pictures don’t need explanation or that using words on screen signals failure. As Dan Roam explains,

A good picture substitutes for the thousand words that are the least necessary.

-- Dan Roam

The trap to avoid is letting the text substitute for you, the presenter. Remember, the slides are a complementary visual channel.

Never send the slides

All this brings us to the series title. I meant for it to be provocative, but I also mean for it to be a principle. If your slides serve as a visual channel that reinforces what you say, they can’t stand alone. If you send them out in advance, you’ll only undermine your storytelling and the humour, intrigue, and impact you expected from your presentation. So, I don’t recommend sending your slides in advance. That said, I want to offer alternatives.

If you want to prepare your audience, send them prep notes. Corporations are busy places, and people struggle to prepare in advance, so the more succinct your prep materials, the more likely people will consume them. One page, a short email, or even a structured instant message can be preparation enough.

If you want to align with your co-presenters, colleagues, or boss before the presentation, then do a dress rehearsal. If a presentation is high-stakes and you don’t have time for a live rehearsal, you could record yourself giving the presentation and send the video out to get feedback. Such feedback can help you solidify your prep and tighten your narrative and delivery. By getting your colleagues and boss onside before an important presentation, you’ll be able to seed your audience with supporters — a pattern Ford, McCollough and Schutta call the “Greek chorus”.

If you want your audience to have some resources handy when you present, create reference materials. You can hand these out as prints before you begin your presentation, or create an online resource. When I deliver presentations online, I often share resources in the chat during the presentation to manage my audience’s cognitive load. The minimalism principle applies here too. Reference materials can become a distraction. The more focused they are, the more effective they’ll be.

And finally, if you want to give your audience something to take away, create a handout that summarises your talk. If you’re diligent about writing presenter notes, a PDF of your slides, juxtaposed with your presenter notes, can serve as a handout for your talk. If I’m speaking at a conference, I often create a single-page takeaway for my audience. When Martin was active on the conference circuit, he shared talk notes for his presentations.

Not every talk needs so many artefacts. It’s your call, based on what you know of your audience. For example, when I presented research findings on the state of remote work at Thoughtworks, I didn’t send any prep notes, but I did create a handout and a dashboard where my audience could play with the raw data. Since the dashboard would be a distraction during the talk, I shared it towards the tail end to let the data provoke questions from the audience.

Figure 5: One presentation. Three artefacts.

Is the approach I’m suggesting a lot of work? Perhaps. If your story is worth telling, and you care about your audience’s experience engaging with you and the impact you make, then it's a worthwhile effort.

Now, do I never send my slides? Never say never, right? There are exceptions. Sometimes my colleagues want to adapt my slides to their narrative. Other times, people are curious about how I built my slides. In such situations, I do share my slides. No problem. Use your judgment to make exceptions when necessary.

Rewrite the rulebook

You’ll notice that I’m asking you to throw away the rulebook that says you should have one slide for every two minutes of speech, or the one that says you need six bullets per slide with no more than six words per bullet. Those are the death-by-PowerPoint rules. Our principles are different.

  • Seek to control the rate of knowledge exposition.
  • Use slides as a visual channel to complement the speaker.
  • Tightly couple the slides and the speaker.
  • Don’t fuss over the number of slides. Slide count doesn’t matter.
  • Be minimalist by default.
  • Treat slides as integrated visuals, not a collection of components.
  • Never send the slides.

And finally, as I explained with the photographs in the “perpetual beta” presentation, we want the visual channels to say a thousand words and blend education and entertainment.

Now that I’ve laid down some principles, let's change tack to “how to” build effective slides. In the next post, we’ll begin with the fundamentals of colours, typography and layouts.
